researcher_notes: Statute text is from ILGA and shows two versions of Sections 6.1, 7.1, 8.1, and 10.2: the text in effect now and the text after P.A. 104-563, which takes effect January 1, 2027. Rules marked 'text in effect before P.A. 104-563' quote the current version. Per the ILGA text, starting 1-1-27 the 7-day police notification rule for sexual offenses is replaced by a 30-day notification window for all crimes, mental health provider evaluations count as notice more broadly, mental health providers who certify a claim are limited to Medicare-approved rates, and emergency awards may cover funeral costs that have been quoted and relocation expenses due to be incurred; re-check these rules after that date. Disagreement: the AG sexual assault FAQ (IL-S7) says relocation covers 'the first month's rent', while the statute (740 ILCS 45/2(h)(7)) says 'the first 2 months' rent'; the statute controls and IL-COV-RELO follows it. The Court of Claims page (IL-S6) still says report within 72 hours without the 7-day sexual assault rule; the statute controls. Late applications may be accepted for good cause (740 ILCS 45/6.1(a-1)); it is not encoded as a rule because it has no fixed time. Expense cap for lost wages uses per='month' because the cap is monthly; the schema's per list has no month value. SASETA: the survivor's insurance is billed but the survivor owes nothing for outpatient exam/treatment; inpatient services may be billed. Insurance-billing param for IL-EXAM-1 is 'allowed' because 410 ILCS 70/7(a)(2) directs billing the survivor's insurer, with an opt-out for survivors who are not the policyholder (7.5(a-5)). Reviewer: the FAQ (IL-S7) also says good cause for a late application will be found when the delay came from a delay in testing a sexual assault kit or matching its DNA profile; the statute (6.1(a-1)) only says 'good cause', so this is not encoded. After the AG finds a claim eligible, the applicant gets 45 days from the letter to submit proof of losses (IL-S4, IL-S7); procedural, not encoded. The general police notification window for non-sexual crimes is 72 hours today (6.1(b)); the 7-day window in IL-REPORT-1 applies to the listed sexual offenses and trafficking. How to file (added): submission methods are online (preferred per the AG page), email of the fillable PDF to CVA@ilag.gov, and mail. The application PDF (IL-S5, Rev. 12/2024) gives two slightly different mailing names at the same address: page 1 says 'Crime Victim Compensation Bureau' and page 10 says 'Crime Victims Services Bureau', both at 115 South LaSalle Street, Chicago, IL 60603; IL-SUBMIT-MAIL uses the page 1 instructions. No fax or in-person filing is stated. The application PDF is fillable with 297 AcroForm fields. Documents are 'if available' at filing; the AG requests the police report itself and asks for proof of losses within 45 days after an eligibility letter. Privacy (added): IL-ACP-1 quotes the AG program page (IL-S9); the statute (IL-S8, 750 ILCS 61/11) says the Attorney General 'shall administer an address confidentiality program for victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking, or stalking', and 61/15 requires a sworn statement that the applicant has good reason to believe they are a victim and fears for their safety. The AG page says the ACP does not require a police report or protective order and cannot keep property records confidential. The ILGA text also shows a version of 750 ILCS 61 as amended by P.A. 104-837, effective 1-1-27, which keeps sexual assault eligibility and adds household members; re-check after that date. IL-RECCONF-1 quotes 740 ILCS 45/4.2 (identical in the text before and after P.A. 104-563); the same section also bars the AG's office from disclosing law enforcement reports and other documentation obtained to investigate a claim to the public.

name: Indiana
program_name: Indiana Violent Crime Victim Compensation Program
agency: Indiana Criminal Justice Institute, Victim Services Division (Victim Compensation Division)
coverage_notes: No separate dollar caps were found for lost wages, medical, security (windows and locks), or emergency shelter; those draw on the $15,000 total. Relocation and travel are listed as non-eligible on the program page, and no statute makes them covered, except emergency shelter care for up to 30 days. No source says whether an exam provider may bill the survivor's insurance; the statutes only bar charging the victim, so insurance_billing is unspecified. The program page links an online application portal but says it currently has problems and asks for written applications; no stable online apply URL was recorded, so apply_url points to the program page. How to file: the program page (IN-S1) gives mail, hand delivery, and fax for the paper application; it says online filing exists but the portal currently has problems and gives no portal URL, so no online submission rule was added. The 'Send written application' email link on that page sits under the hospital sexual assault claim section, not the survivor application, so no email rule was added. The program page says medical bills and police reports are not needed at filing; the documents listed come from what the program says it collects or requires to pay (IN-S1, 203 IAC 1-1-4). Processing time: only the statutory 30-day payment window after an award is computed (IC 5-2-6.1-43(b)); the FAQ's 'within a few months' has no number.
researcher_notes: Statute text is from Justia's 2025 Indiana Code (the official iga.in.gov code viewer is a script app); the administrative rule is from the official Indiana Administrative Register. Conflicts, statute wins in the rules: (1) Filing deadline: IC 5-2-6.1-16(b) requires the application within 180 days of the crime, extendable for good cause to no more than two years; the program page says applications must be filed no later than two years after the crime. (2) Total cap: IC 5-2-6.1-35 caps an award at $15,000; the FAQ describes $20,000 total ($15,000 plus an additional $5,000 for funeral costs). Funeral costs up to $5,000 are a listed expense in IC 5-2-6.1-21.1(d)(6). (3) Medical expense window: IC 5-2-6.1-21.1(d) covers expenses incurred within 180 days, extendable to two years; the program page says medical expenses must be incurred within two years. (4) The application form State Form 23776 (R14 / 9-21) predates the 2022 changes: it lists a 180-day deadline and a 72-hour report with no sexual assault exam alternative. (5) 203 IAC 1 (readopted 2023) still contains older figures superseded by statute: a 48-hour reporting rule, a $4,000 funeral cap, $1,000 or $1,500 counseling caps, and a 48-hour report condition for sex crime ER payment; it also says a provider may bill the patient or a collateral source if fund payment is denied (203 IAC 1-2-1(c)), which conflicts with IC 16-21-8-6(f) and IC 16-21-8-1(a) (exam services may not depend on reporting to or cooperating with law enforcement). Only the $500 emergency award is taken from 203 IAC 1, since no statute addresses emergency awards; the FAQ confirms emergency funding exists and that an application must be filed first. (6) The program page says crimes outside Indiana are not eligible; IC 5-2-6.1-12(a)(1)(B) lets Indiana residents apply for crimes in places without a substantially similar program. Other: victims of a child sex crime may apply until age 31 (IC 5-2-6.1-16(e)) and are exempt from the 72-hour report rule (IC 5-2-6.1-17(a)). IC 5-2-6.1-21.1(f) bars a health care provider that accepts division payment from charging the victim a copayment. Bodily injury includes emotional trauma that stems directly from a physical impairment, visible injury, or physical pain (IC 5-2-6.1-0.5). IN-S16 (IC 5-2-6.1-43, payment timing), IN-S20 (IC 16-21-8-1, list of sex crimes), and IN-S22 (rights brochure) are saved for context. Reviewer additions: 203 IAC 1-1-9(d) also says the total award may not exceed $15,000 per victim, which agrees with IC 5-2-6.1-35 against the FAQ's $20,000. IC 16-21-8-5(b) conditions payment for additional forensic services (not the exam itself) on the victim being 18 or older or, for a minor, a report to child protective services or law enforcement, the crime occurring in Indiana, and the provider starting the claim in the division's web system. IC 5-2-6.1-16(g) gives victims of battery on a child under 14 five years to apply. How-to-file additions: application_form is IN-S3, State Form 23776 (R14 / 9-21), the PDF the program page currently links; it has 89 AcroForm fields (the PDF is AES-encrypted with an empty user password). 203 IAC 1-1-3(a)(2) says claims are filed in person or by certified mail; the program page adds fax. A Spanish application is linked from the program page but not saved. Privacy additions: the Address Confidentiality Program is run by the Office of the Indiana Attorney General (IN-S23). The page says survivors of sexual assault are eligible ('Survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, harassment, intimidation and invasion of privacy who fear for their safety are eligible for the ACP'); the quoted sentence in the rule has a missing comma after 'sexual assault' on the page itself. Mail goes to a substitute address and is forwarded, and the substitute address is used for driver's license, vehicle, voter, and school registrations and legal process. Applicants must be 18 or older, or a parent or guardian applying for a minor or a guardian for an incapacitated person; IC 5-26.5-2-1 (IN-S24, saved for context) also lists emancipated minors. The application must be signed by a trained victim advocate. Record confidentiality rests on IC 5-2-6.1-11.5 (IN-S25), which makes a claimant's personal information and medical records confidential; the program FAQ (IN-S2) adds that information is given only to the legal applicant unless the victim or claimant gives written authorization to speak to a third party.

name: Kansas
agency: Office of the Kansas Attorney General, Division of Crime Victims Compensation (Crime Victims Compensation Board)

coverage_notes: No minimum-loss threshold was found. Instead K.S.A. 74-7305(e) requires the board to find financial stress (the claimant cannot keep their customary level of health, safety and education without undue financial hardship), judged on dependents, living expenses, special needs, income, resources and other factors. researcher_notes: The compiled K.S.A. 65-448(h) on the legislature site (KS-S7) still says the county pays the exam fee, but the page flags 2026 HB 2613 as an enacted measure affecting the section. The enrolled HB 2613 (KS-S8) moves the fee to the Crime Victims Compensation Board, and the AG page (KS-S1) and SAFE invoice (KS-S3) say the program pays for exams from July 1, 2026. The rules use the newer law for the payer; the no-billing sentence is the same in both versions. The enrolled-bill PDF text mixes struck and inserted words, so quotes from it are limited to new text that reads cleanly. K.A.R. 20-2-6 (1993) still lists only a 72-hour police report; it was not used because the later statute, K.S.A. 74-7305(f), adds the forensic exam alternative. The ten-year deadline in 74-7305(b)(2)(C)(ii) applies to a 'sexually violent crime as defined in K.S.A. 22-3717'. Reviewer fetched 22-3717 (KS-S11): (d)(5) lists rape (21-5503), aggravated criminal sodomy, criminal sodomy under 21-5504(a)(3)-(4) only, aggravated sexual battery (21-5505(b)), child sex offenses, aggravated incest and attempts. Plain sexual battery (21-5505(a)) is not on the list, so those survivors get the general five-year limit. The SAFE invoice also tells providers survivors may apply whether or not they report to law enforcement. The OVC state directory lists the same phone (785-296-2359) and website. Reviewer: the 74-7301 page (KS-S5) lists 2026 HB 2780 (terramation) as an enacted measure affecting that section; it likely touches the funeral wording in 74-7301(a), and the amended text was not fetched, so KS-CAP-7 reflects the compiled pre-amendment text. The no-billing rule now cites the enrolled HB 2613 text (KS-S8) instead of the superseded compiled 65-448 (KS-S7); the sentence is identical. How to file: the application (KS-S2, revised May 2025, the version linked from the board page) has 202 fillable AcroForm fields but no mail-to address, online portal, email or fax instruction. The only filing destination in the official sources is the Contact block on the board page (KS-S1), so KS-SUBMIT-1 uses that mailing address. The same block lists a fax number, (785) 296-0652, and a generic 'Send us an email' form; neither is stated as a way to file an application, so no fax or email submission rule was added. The SAFE invoice (KS-S3) also lists that fax, but its submission instructions are for exam providers, not survivors. No online application was found. No photo ID or police report copy is requested; the form asks only for the police report number. Safe at Home: the AG program page (KS-S12) says the program gives a substitute address for use with state and local agencies and free first-class mail forwarding; K.S.A. 75-455 (KS-S15) requires state and local agencies to accept the substitute address unless the AG finds a bona fide statutory need for the real one. Eligibility (KS-S14) also requires being 18 or older (or a parent or guardian applying for a minor or incapacitated person), living at or moving to an address unknown to the perpetrator, and naming the AG as agent for service of process and mail. Certification lasts four years. Banks and private utilities do not have to accept the substitute address. The enroll param keeps the source's wording except that the curly apostrophe in 'Attorney General's' was written as ASCII. Record confidentiality: the compiled 74-7308 (KS-S13) does not yet show 2026 HB 2613; the enrolled bill (KS-S8, sec. 3) keeps the same confidentiality sentence as (e)(1) and adds discovery and disclosure exceptions: the board may share records with law enforcement, county or district attorneys, and the Kansas Department for Children and Families to help a child abuse or neglect investigation, and with law enforcement when it finds records false or fraudulent; those two exceptions expire July 1, 2031 unless reenacted. Existing exceptions remain for appeals, in-camera court review after a strict showing, and board orders granting or denying compensation. The application (KS-S2) also says all information provided is confidential under K.S.A. 74-7308.

name: Kentucky
agency: Public Protection Cabinet, Office of Claims and Appeals, Crime Victims Compensation Board
coverage_not_found: ["filing_deadline","reporting_requirement","minimum_loss","expense_cap:counseling (time limit of two years only, no dollar cap)","expense_cap:transportation","expense_cap:medical (overall cap only)"]
coverage_notes: Filing deadline and police report rule: 2024 Ky. Acts ch. 67 (SB 319, effective July 15, 2024) deleted the old five-year filing limit from KRS 49.330 and the old 48-hour report rule. The current KRS 49.330 and 49.370 text sets no general filing deadline and no reporting deadline, so no filing_deadline or reporting_requirement rule is recorded. The CVCB FAQ (updated August 2024) still lists a police report of the incident among the documents generally required with a claim, and the claim form asks when and to whom the crime was reported, so a survivor should expect to be asked for one; the program brochure says the sexual assault exam program does not require reporting. No minimum loss amount was found. The program's HTML pages (static_id=158 and 159) could not be saved because the fetch tool strips their ASP.NET form content; their PDFs were saved instead.
researcher_notes: Caps come from KRS 49.370 as amended effective July 15, 2024 and match the CVCB FAQ cap list ($50,000 overall, $500 per week lost earnings, $2,000 relocation, $2,000 temporary housing, $10,000 funeral, $1,000 emergency). Relocation and temporary housing apply only when the crime happened at the victim's primary residence. The SAEP FAQ (revised 11/2023) predates the 2024 and 2025 amendments: its dollar fee schedule (citing 107 KAR 2:010) is superseded by 802 KAR 3:020 Medicaid-rate caps, and its statements that incomplete exams and same-day ambulance or triage are not paid conflict with current KRS 216B.400(10), which bars charging the victim for exams whether or not completed and for same-day triage and ambulance. Only its insurance-billing answer is used (KY-EXAM-4), and that matches the current program web page, which says providers bill insurance first. Under KRS 49.340(4) claims are investigated whether or not the offender is caught, charged, or convicted. Emergency award requests are limited to one per claimant by the program's January 2025 policy (KY-S21). Reviewer note: the live exam program page (static_id=159, read with curl but not saveable by fetch_source.py, which returns blocked or empty even with --chrome) says providers bill private or public insurance first, matching KY-EXAM-4, but it also says the victim may be charged for expenses not related to the exam process such as ambulance and triage. That conflicts with current KRS 216B.400(10)(d), which bars charging the victim for same-day triage and ambulance costs, so the statute (KY-EXAM-2) controls. How to file: 802 KAR 3:010 Section 4(2) lists in person or private delivery, mail, email (if the claim fits in one email), and the online portal; fax (502-573-4817) comes from the CVCB FAQ only, not the regulation. The paper application (KY-S19, revised July 2024, still the version linked on the program page on Oct 3, 2026) is a flat PDF with no AcroForm fields, so it must be printed or filled by hand. Document rules come from 802 KAR 3:010 and 3:030 and the program's 'Documents to include' checklist (KY-S22). The program page also links a 'How to file a claim' PDF, but that URL returned 404 on Oct 3, 2026, so it is not saved. Processing time: the regulation sets a 90-day deadline for the investigative report on claims filed after July 1, 2026 (120 days for claims filed after July 1, 2025); no source states a time for the Board's final decision or payment, and the brochure says processing time depends on several factors. Missing documentation: under 802 KAR 3:010 Section 10 a claim goes into default if required documents are not sent within 90 days, and can be revived without a new application. Claimants get access to the online tracking portal within one week of filing. Privacy: Kentucky's address confidentiality program is the Safe at Home Program in the Office of the Secretary of State (KRS 14.300 to 14.318). KRS 14.302 names sexual assault, rape, and other sexual crimes among the offenses it protects against, and KRS 14.304(3) says applicants file with the Secretary of State, either with an application assistant or online through the Secretary of State's portal; KRS 14.304(7) also exempts applicant and participant addresses from the Open Records Act. The saved KRS 14.302 and 14.304 texts are marked 'Effective until January 1, 2027', so an amended version takes effect then and should be rechecked. The Secretary of State's Safe at Home web pages could not be saved (the fetch tool returned blocked or empty, also with --chrome), so the statutes are used. Record confidentiality comes from 802 KAR 3:010 Section 5, the claim tracking portal section; no separate statute making compensation claim records confidential was found among the saved KRS 49 sections.

name: Louisiana
program_name: Crime Victims' Compensation (formerly Crime Victims Reparations)
agency: Louisiana Commission on Law Enforcement and Administration of Criminal Justice (LCLE), Crime Victims' Compensation Board
statute_citation: La. R.S. 46:1801 to 46:1822 (Crime Victims' Compensation Act, as amended by Acts 2026, No. 684, effective Aug. 1, 2026); La. R.S. 40:1216.1; LAC 22:XIII
coverage_notes: I found no minimum loss rule in the statute, the LAC rules, or the program pages. Nothing I saved covers home security devices or lock changes. Lost wages are paid at 80 percent of the gross weekly wage with no separate dollar cap I could find. Mileage is paid at the state travel rate, which is not stated as a number in the rule. Medical bills have no separate dollar cap beyond the $15,000 total; the board pays up to 70 percent of unpaid balances. The insurance_billing value for the exam is prohibited only in the program's provider instructions (LA-S3); the statute itself says the survivor cannot be billed directly or indirectly and does not mention insurance. Reviewer: the LAC 22:XIII.503(F) ambulance limits ($300 ground, $500 air) exist but are not encoded as a transportation cap, since ambulance is billed as medical. Record confidentiality: I found no statute or rule that makes the compensation board's claim files as a whole confidential or exempt from the Public Records Law. The rule I encoded is La. R.S. 46:1844(W), which bars public agencies, naming the board, from publicly disclosing the name, address, contact information, or identity of sex offense victims; it protects identity, not the whole claim file.
researcher_notes: Big change: Acts 2026, No. 684 (HB 969, signed by the Governor, effective Aug. 1, 2026 per the Resume Digest) rewrote La. R.S. 46:1801 to 1822. It renamed the program from Crime Victims Reparations to Crime Victims' Compensation, moved the filing deadline from one year to three years from the date of the crime, rewrote 'reasonable documentation' (law enforcement report, court records, a healthcare provider attestation, or a forensic exam attestation), added sexually oriented criminal offenses to the covered crimes, kept the $15,000 cap ($25,000 for permanent and total disability) and the $1,000 emergency award, removed catastrophic property loss, and added temporary lodging or permanent relocation and clothing/bedding/evidence property to pecuniary loss. As of Oct 3, 2026 the legislature's Law.aspx pages and Justia (2025) still show the pre-Act text, so I quoted the enrolled Act (LA-S14) or its official Resume Digest (LA-S15). The enrolled Act PDF prints struck-through deletions inline in its extracted text, so I detected strikethrough lines with PyMuPDF and only quoted lines with no struck words; its text also carries line numbers, so Act quotes are one printed line each. Re-snapshot the codified statute once legis.la.gov updates. Stale official material that conflicts with the statute (statute wins): the program page (LA-S1), the application form (LA-S2, Feb 2025), and LAC 22:XIII (Feb 2025) still say one year to file; the program page still lists vacation and sick leave as sources that pay first, but Act 684 excludes vacation and sick leave from wage continuation collateral sources; the program page still mentions catastrophic property loss of a residence, which Act 684 removed; the application form says insurance must be billed first, but LAC 22:XIII.303(A)(5) lets sexual offense victims choose whether to use private insurance or Medicaid. Sexual assault specifics: under 46:1809(B)(3)(b) as amended, the no-award grounds for failing to cooperate with law enforcement or being the offender/accessory do not apply when the application results from a sexually oriented criminal offense; the behavior-based reduction in 46:1809(B)(4)(a) also does not apply to those victims. The pre-Act 46:1806(B)(2) sentence that sexual offense victims need not report to police was removed by Act 684; non-report applications now rely on the reasonable documentation list, and LAC 22:XIII.303(A)(2)(c) still says adult victims need not report. LAC 22:XIII.303(A)(1) says applications for adult sexual offense victims go straight to the board office instead of the parish sheriff. Forensic exam: 40:1216.1(A)(6) says the survivor cannot be billed directly or indirectly; the provider ($600) and facility ($1,000) are paid under 46:1822, which Act 684 changed so LCLE staff, not a board order, approve exam reimbursements within 30 days. Services outside the forensic exam itself (for example treatment of injuries) may be billed to the patient or insurance per LA-S3, and the survivor can then seek compensation for them. Under 40:1216.1(A)(1)(a), no hospital or provider may require a survivor to report to police to get care or evidence collection. HB 998 (2026), which would have allowed exam billing through the patient's insurance, did not pass. Phone: the program lists 1-888-6-VICTIM, which spells 888-684-2846, the same number in the OVC directory; the office line is (225) 342-1749. Online applications are listed as coming soon on the CVC Claims page. Reviewer (Oct 3): corrected the exam payment pinpoint to LAC 22:XIII.503(A)(3) (it was 501(B)(3)); moved the child care rule from a program-page list fragment to the amended statute 46:1802(16)(c); confirmed with PyMuPDF strike detection that the 3-year deadline, the board extension clause, the $15,000 cap line, the $1,000 emergency award line, (A)(3) of 46:1805 and the 46:1809(B)(3)(b) and (B)(4)(a) sexual offense exceptions are unstruck. Open points: the program page still says victims must cooperate fully with law enforcement, which 46:1809(B)(3)(b) no longer applies to sexual offense applications; the Act does not say whether the 3-year period reaches crimes committed before Aug. 1, 2026 whose 1-year period had already run; LAC 22:XIII.503(Q)(3) says a police or incident report should accompany a relocation claim, which may matter for survivors who did not report; LAC 22:XIII.301(A)(2)(b)(i) says insurance must be processed before mental health claims, which sits uneasily with the 303(A)(5) insurance choice for sexual offense claims; Act 684 also removed the board's permissive rulemaking power, so how long the Feb 2025 LAC rules stay in force is unclear. How to file (Oct 3): the application PDF (LA-S2, Feb 19, 2025, still the one linked from the Downloads page as of its Aug 2026 update) has no fillable fields, so it is printed and filled by hand. Mail is the only method I could confirm. LAC 22:XIII.303(A)(1) says applications may also be filed online at the board's website, but the CVC Claims page (LA-S16) lists CVC Online Applications as Coming Soon, so I did not add an online submission rule; recheck later. No email, fax, or in-person filing address is stated. Adult sexual offense applications go straight to the board office (P.O. Box 3133, Baton Rouge, LA 70821) rather than the parish sheriff. Required documents: the form's reasonable documentation list (police report, court records, sworn certifications) is the pre-Act version; I used the Act 684 Resume Digest list instead (law enforcement report, court records, a healthcare provider attestation, or a forensic exam attestation). The form's 'insurance must be billed before claims are submitted' line conflicts with LAC 22:XIII.303(A)(5) for sexual offense victims, so I did not add an insurance_statement document. The 30 to 45 day processing time is the program page's typical time for the sheriff's eligibility decision, not a payment deadline. Privacy additions (Oct 3, 2026): The Address Confidentiality Program is run by the Secretary of State under La. R.S. 44:51 to 57; the program page (LA-S17) and R.S. 44:52(A)(1) and (A)(3)(a) (LA-S18, Justia 2025 text) both say victims of sexual assault are eligible. The page also says applicants must have relocated to an address with no public record and must not own the home, and R.S. 44:52(A)(4)(e) says participants who are registered voters give up in-person voting and vote absentee by mail. Certification lasts four years per R.S. 44:52(B)(2). For record confidentiality I quoted the 2025 Justia text of R.S. 46:1844(W)(1)(a) (LA-S19), which still says 'Crime Victims Reparations Board'; Act 684 (LA-S14, page 40) only renames it to the Crime Victims' Compensation Board and leaves the duty unchanged. I did not quote the Act because its extracted text mixes struck words into those lines. Hearings before the board are open to the public unless the board closes them in the victim's interest (R.S. 46:1808(B) as amended), which is worth telling survivors.

name: Massachusetts
program_name: Victim Compensation Program (Massachusetts Victims of Violent Crime Compensation)
agency: Massachusetts Office for Victim Assistance (MOVA)
coverage_notes: No minimum loss and no emergency or advance award appear in M.G.L. c. 258C or 124 CMR 2.00. Counseling, lost wages and medical have no separate dollar caps; they fall under the $25,000 total cap (124 CMR 2.06(5)(a) only allows the agency to ask for updated verification after six months or 30 sessions, which is not a cap). Relocation, temporary housing and childcare are not listed as compensable in the statute, the regulations, or the program page; the program page says other losses are not covered, so they are treated as not found rather than recorded as a rule.
researcher_notes: Administration moved from the Attorney General's Victim Compensation and Assistance Division to MOVA effective July 1, 2025 (St. 2025, c. 9); the statute pages show both versions and the quotes use the text effective July 1, 2025. 124 CMR 2.00 (effective 8/4/25, Mass. Register #1564) replaces the AG's former 940 CMR rules; a scanned 'emergency regulations' PDF linked from the program page had no extractable text and was not used. The exam billing guidance (MA-S12, 2018) and the SAECK brochure (MA-S14) still name the AG's office and an older 617-727-2200 number; current contact is MOVA at 617-586-1340. Exam rules come from regulation 124 CMR 2.06(15) and state agency guidance; I found no Massachusetts statute that by itself bars billing the survivor for the exam. Under the 2018 guidance, direct hospital billing applies to ED care when the assault occurred in Massachusetts and a kit was administered; ambulance, inpatient and follow-up care go through the survivor's own application. The DPH SANE page says patients who decline the kit must report to police within five days and attach the report. Claimants must also cooperate with law enforcement unless they have a reasonable excuse (c. 258C s. 2(c)); 124 CMR 2.05(6)(b) says the physical or psychological impact of the crime or reasonable fear for safety can be a reasonable excuse. M.G.L. c. 258C s. 14 and 124 CMR 2.10 bar health care providers with notice of a claim from debt collection while it is pending. The regulation's internal cross-references in 2.05 are misnumbered (subsections start at (4)); pinpoints use the numbering as printed. Reviewer note: 124 CMR 2.05(7)(b) adds a further minor-victim extension (if a criminal complaint or indictment issues after the victim turns 18, the filing period starts on that date); no schema 'from' value fits it, so it is recorded here and not as a rule. 124 CMR 2.05(5)(a) also counts a report as timely if made within five days of when the crime was discovered or reasonably should have been discovered. How to file (added Oct 3): the saved application MA-S4 is still the English form linked from the program page (same 237.85 KB file; PDF metadata 'Victim Comp App 2026_English', modified July 2026) and has 107 fillable AcroForm fields. The program pages (MA-S1, MA-S2) say completed applications must be submitted by email, fax, or mail; the address, fax and email come from the form's return block on page 4. Discrepancy: the form prints the email as VCCorrespondence@state.ma.us, while the program pages list the Victim Compensation email as VCCorrespondence@mass.gov; MA-SUB-3 follows the form, and a survivor emailing should know both are official. No online or in-person filing method is stated (a Northampton office exists at 403 Pleasant Street but no source says to file there). Documents: the form asks for copies of bills and/or receipts for each expense checked; the police report is needed only when the survivor declined the kit or was outside the kit window (DPH SANE protocol, which still names VCAD); employer wage verification and a provider disability letter are on request for lost wages. Homemaker, dependency and funeral claims have their own proof rules in 124 CMR 2.06 that are not encoded. Processing time: MOVA says decisions generally take 4 to 6 months; the range minimum is stored as min_months. Privacy (added Oct 3): The Address Confidentiality Program is run by the Secretary of the Commonwealth under M.G.L. c. 9A (the statute page URL I tried returned a 404, so the rule uses the official program pages). MA-S17 says 'If you are a survivor of domestic violence, sexual assault, rape, or stalking, you may apply'; enrollment goes through a trained application assistant (found via 1-866-SAFE-ADD), who submits the application, and the applicant must relocate to an address the perpetrator does not know and not disclose it to any state or local agency. Participants also get confidential voter registration, and MA-S17 says 'All ACP records are strictly confidential.' Record confidentiality comes from 124 CMR 2.09; the application's MOVA Victim Compensation Confidentiality Statement (MA-S4) and the DPH SANE page (MA-S13) say the same, the latter adding that records cannot be released without the claimant's consent or as a matter of law.

name: Maryland
agency: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy, Criminal Injuries Compensation Board
statute_citation: Md. Code, Crim. Proc. 11-801 to 11-819; exam payment at 11-1007
coverage_notes: conduct_reduction: the 2024 Victim Compensation Reform Act (Ch. 705, HB 575, MD-S12, Section 1 effective July 1, 2025) struck the old contributory-conduct reduction and the provocation bar from 11-810; the current 11-801 to 11-819 text has no conduct reduction. The program page (MD-S8) and 2021 application (MD-S9) still describe contributory conduct as a ground for ineligibility, so no rule was written. excluded_expense: the only exclusion list found is in the 2021 application instructions, and most of it (property loss, lock changes, relocation, child care, mileage) is contradicted by current statute, so it was not used. No dollar caps were found for relocation or transportation. Exam insurance billing: the statute (11-1007) does not mention insurance, but COMAR 10.12.02.05A(2)-(3) (MD-S13) bars billing the victim, family, or private insurance for any difference and requires providers to accept state payment in full, so insurance_billing is prohibited in MD-EXAM-5. processing_time: no saved source states a time for a decision or payment; 11-809(b)(2) only requires the Board to notify the claimant within 10 days after receiving a claim, which is an acknowledgment, not a decision, so no rule was written. record_confidentiality: no law makes CICB claims confidential. Criminal Procedure 11-806(a) (MD-S16) says the opposite: 'the record of a proceeding before the Board or a Board member is a public record'; 11-806(b) only keeps confidential a record or report the Board obtains whose confidentiality is already protected by other law (for example medical records). COMAR 12.01.01.12 (MD-S11) only subjects non-claimant review to Public Information Act limits, requires secure handling of documents about children, and bars disclosing full Social Security, driver's license and similar numbers. No rule was written.
researcher_notes: Statute text is from the Maryland General Assembly site, which reflects HB 575 (2024 Ch. 705). Per Sections 3 and 4 of Ch. 705 (MD-S12), Section 1 (the 11-801 to 11-819 amendments, including the struck 48-hour report, cooperation, and contributory-conduct rules and the new caps) took effect July 1, 2025; only Section 2 took effect July 1, 2024. Claims tied to crimes or decisions before July 1, 2025 may have been handled under the old rules. Several agency materials are out of date and statutes win: (1) Filing deadline: statute 11-809 says 4 years; the 2021 application (MD-S9) says three years. (2) Police report: the old 48-hour reporting and full-cooperation requirements were struck by HB 575 (MD-S12); current 11-810(b) makes a police report one of several accepted kinds of evidence. The program page (MD-S8) and the application still say to report within 48 hours and list a police report for all claims, so a survivor may still be asked for one in practice. (3) Emergency award: statute 11-813 says up to $10,000; COMAR 12.01 (MD-S11) still says $2,000 per claim and asks for a police report for an emergency award. (4) Covered expenses: statute now covers one-time relocation, child care for care visits, travel to care, and property repair or replacement including locks; the 2021 application lists these as not covered. (5) Phone: OVC directory and the application list 410-585-3010 for CICB; the program page lists 410-697-9338 under the CICB address. The application also names the agency the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy; the website domain is gocpp.maryland.gov. MD-CAP-5 maps lost earnings to the disability-related cap because 11-811(a) pays lost earnings under the workers' compensation disability schedule (two-thirds of average wage). (6) Exam regulation: COMAR 10.12.02 (MD-S13) still names the Maryland Department of Health as payer and was last amended in 2008; the statute now names GOCPP, and the SARU page (MD-S10) says SARU operates under COMAR 10.12.02. COMAR 10.12.02.03B says a forensic exam is performed within 120 hours with a police report or property-held number, while statute 11-1007(c)(1) covers exams within 15 days; the statute wins, and SARU FAQ says the exam is covered without a police report. (7) Counseling caps: the $10,000 per claimant / $20,000 per incident counseling cap in 11-811(b)(6) applies only to household family members of an injured victim, so it is recorded as MD-COV-10 (covered_expense with applies_to) rather than an expense_cap, to keep it from capping the victim's own counseling at $10,000. The victim's own counseling falls under the $45,000 cap in MD-CAP-3. (8) How to file: the linked application (MD-S9, rev. Nov 2021, still the English application linked from the program page on Oct 3 2026) is a fillable PDF with 135 AcroForm fields. Its instruction sheet says to mail, email, or deliver the completed application to the CICB office, which gives the mail, email, and in-person rules; statute 11-809(b)(1) (MD-S3) also allows filing in person, by mail, or electronically, and COMAR 12.01 (MD-S11) still says in person or by regular mail. The application header lists a fax number, (410) 764-3815, but no source says applications may be faxed, so no fax rule was written. There is no online submission portal; the 'fillable Online Application' in the instructions is the fillable PDF. Address conflict: the application prints Ste. 206, while the current program page footer (MD-S8) lists Suite 209 at the same street address with phone 410-697-9338; the submission rules use the application's address because that is the document that gives the filing instruction, and a survivor may want to confirm the suite by phone. Required documents come from the instruction sheet's Benefits & Required Documentation list; the police report item predates HB 575 (see note 2). The application does not ask for a photo ID, proof of residency, or the forensic exam record. (9) Address confidentiality: the program is set up by State Gov't 7-301 to 7-312; 7-302 (purpose) says participants use an address designated by the Office of the Secretary of State as a substitute address, and 7-304 lets an applicant qualify with their own statement of fear (no police report needed). The enroll text comes from the Secretary of State's Apply to ACP page (MD-S15). That page is built on SharePoint and its body sits inside a form element, so the fetch tool's .txt snapshot holds only the translation disclaimer; the enroll wording was read from the saved raw HTML (rules/sources/MD/MD-S15.html). The same page says the ACP serves people who have recently relocated or will relocate within 30 days and cannot redact an address that is already public, and that applying may take up to 10 business days. The older Safe at Home brochure on sos.maryland.gov still describes the program as only for domestic violence and human trafficking victims; the statute (7-303, MD-S14) and the current Apply page both include sexual assault. (10) Record confidentiality: Maryland treats the record of a CICB proceeding as a public record (11-806(a), MD-S16); only records already confidential under other law stay confidential (11-806(b)). Survivors should not assume their claim file is closed to the public; the ACP substitute address can keep the home address off it.

agency: Office of the Maine Attorney General, Victims' Compensation Board

coverage_not_found: ["minimum_loss","emergency_award","expense_cap for counseling","expense_cap for lost_wages","expense_cap for relocation","expense_cap for transportation","expense_cap for security","application_pdf_url","processing_time"]
coverage_notes: No minimum loss, emergency award, or per-expense dollar caps for counseling, lost wages, relocation, transportation or security were found in the statute (5 M.R.S. ch. 316-A), the Board rules (26-550 ch. 3, 6, 8), or the AG program pages. researcher_notes: Statute text is from legislature.maine.gov (page says data extracted 10/23/2025, so it includes PL 2025 c. 109 and c. 171). Relocation was added to eligible expenses by PL 2025 c. 171. The AG's Program Law and History page (ME-S4) still mentions an older $500 forensic exam maximum; the statute (3360-M(2)) and the current SAFE page both say $750, so the rules use $750. The exam payment covers only the exam and related testing and treatment; the SAFE page says hospitals may bill the survivor or insurer for unrelated charges such as x-rays, which can then be claimed through a regular application (police report required). Board rule 26-550 ch. 8 (2000) also still says $500 and covers only gross sexual assault, while the statute now covers any Title 17-A chapter 11 crime; statute wins. Board rule 26-550 ch. 6 sets the 75% medical guideline and requires exhausting insurance first; the rule files are .doc and could not be saved with the fetch tool, so the 75% rule is quoted from the AG page instead. Toll-free victim line on ME-S5: 1-800-903-7882. Separate from this program, Maine has a Victims' Property Compensation Fund (5 M.R.S. 3360-S, saved as ME-S13) that can pay up to $1,000 for unreimbursed property losses from a crime occurring on or after Jan 1, 2022, with its own 5-day report and 3-year filing rules; it is not encoded as a rule here because the main program excludes property, but a survivor whose phone or belongings were taken or damaged may want to apply there. The 3-year filing clock runs from the injury or compensable loss, encoded as from=crime. Reviewer (Oct 3): ME-EXAM-3 recategorized from exam_payment to reporting_requirement (required=false, expense forensic_exam), matching how other states encode 'no report needed for the exam'. Added ME-EXAM-5 from the SAFE page: direct billing applies only when a sexual assault evidence kit is used; without a kit the provider bills normally, so the no-bill protection depends on a kit being used. ME-EXAM-4 quote extended to include that unrelated charges such as x-rays may be billed. The SAFE page's provider notice still says 'gross sexual assault', while 3360-M(1) now covers any Title 17-A chapter 11 crime; statute wins. How to file (Oct 3): Maine has no downloadable paper application; the AG program page links only to the online portal (https://mainevcp.heart4victims.org/), and the AG 'Apply for Victim's Compensation' online-services page is just a link with no text, so program.application_form is set to source_id null, fillable false, field_count 0. The portal is a script-only app and could not be saved. The Program Law and History page (ME-S4) says a paper form is available from the program office and District Attorneys' Victim Witness Advocate Programs and must be signed and sent to the Board, but no mailing address, fax, or email for the program is published on the saved pages (the AG contact page lists only the office's general address and the program phone numbers), so no mail, fax, or email submission rule was added. Required documents come from 5 M.R.S. 3360-D(1)(B)-(D) and the counseling guidelines. No processing time is stated; ME-S4 only says a complete claim is reviewed at the Board's next monthly meeting, which is not encoded as a number. Privacy (Oct 3): Maine's Address Confidentiality Program is in 5 M.R.S. 90-B (saved as ME-S14), run by the Secretary of State; it covers victims of sexual assault, and applications go through a registered application assistant, and the participant's application and supporting materials are not public records (90-B(7)). Certification lasts 4 years. Compensation records are confidential under 5 M.R.S. 3360-D(4) (ME-S9), but the AG may disclose them at its discretion to law enforcement, courts and Corrections for restitution, a claimant in a hearing or appeal, or others to carry out the chapter; Tend should tell survivors their file is not fully sealed from police. 3360-S (ME-S13) has a parallel confidentiality clause for the Victims' Property Compensation Fund.

name: Michigan
agency: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, Division of Victim Services, Crime Victim Services Commission
coverage_not_found: ["reporting_requirement.within_days","expense_cap.medical (no separate medical cap found; medical is limited only by the $45,000 aggregate)","administrative rules setting caps or rates (none saved)","processing_time"]
coverage_notes: No statutory time limit for reporting to police was found in MCL 18.360 or the program pages saved here, so within_days is left out. Michigan administrative rules were not searched or saved; all caps come from MCL 18.361, 18.359, and 18.355a. Counseling has two hourly rates (therapist/counselor vs psychologist/physician), recorded as separate expense_cap rules. No processing time is stated in the saved program pages, application, checklist, or reference guide; the checklist only says timely submission of documents may reduce processing time, so no processing_time rule was added. Address confidentiality: Michigan's ACP (Address Confidentiality Program Act, 2020 PA 301, MCL 780.851 et seq.) is run by the Department of Attorney General; MCL 780.855 (MI-S22) and the AG pages (MI-S20, MI-S21) name sexual assault victims as eligible. Record confidentiality: MCL 18.363 makes a claimant's file and testimony exempt from FOIA, though the record of a commission proceeding is otherwise a public record.
researcher_notes: Statute text is from legislature.mi.gov (current through 2022 PA 77 and 78, effective Aug. 12, 2023). The MDHHS SAFE Response page says that for injuries other than the forensic exam, a victim 'would have to' report to police to get compensation, while MCL 18.355a(10) says a forensic exam satisfies prompt reporting and cooperation for payments under section 6, and the MDHHS Do I Qualify page says an exam may be used in lieu of a police report. The statute wins; Tend should rely on MI-REPORT-1. MCL 18.355a(10) also says a survivor cannot be required to participate in the criminal justice system or cooperate with law enforcement to receive a forensic exam. The minimum-loss waiver for criminal sexual conduct is discretionary ('may waive'). Security cap is per residence and crime scene cleanup cap is per crime scene, so params.per uses 'residence' and 'crime_scene', which are not in the schema's per list. The FAQ and brochure say the program does not cover pain and suffering; the forensic exam payment to providers is capped at $1,200 (with up to $700 of that for facility and exam fees) and is separate from the victim's own compensation claim. The federal OVC directory lists the compensation office line as 517-241-7373; the victims-only toll-free line 877-251-7373 is on the MDHHS program page. Reviewer: the saved sources do not say whether the $45,000 aggregate cap and the 2022 PA 77 caps apply to crimes that happened before Aug. 12, 2023 (the agency page says the limit was recently raised from $25,000). MI-CAP-4 (agency table) matches the statutory 35-session and 20-family-session limits in MCL 18.361(6). Filing: the Applying for Compensation page says applications should be submitted electronically when possible, by email (MDHHS-MichiganCrimeVictim@Michigan.gov) or fax (517-335-2439), and can still be mailed; there is no online portal and no in-person drop-off is stated. The application PDF (DCH-0560, Rev. 1-26, MI-S15) is fillable with 202 AcroForm fields and says the previous edition may be used. Required documents come from the English Application Checklist (Revised 02/2025, MI-S18); several apply only to specific benefits (relocation, lost earnings, funeral, loss of support), so each required_document rule carries an expense or note saying when it applies. The checklist also lists two cost estimates and a prescription for rehabilitative equipment if disabled by the injury; that item was not added as a separate rule. ACP: eligibility also requires that the applicant be changing residence (MCL 780.855(2); 'Planning to move' on the AG page) and not be on the sex offender registry; applications must be made with a certified application assistant or victim advocate and include a notarized statement. The AG page's enrollment text says 'with the assistant of' (a typo in the source); the enroll param keeps it as written. MCL 18.363 says the record of a proceeding before the commission is a public record; only the claimant's file and testimony are FOIA-exempt, so Tend should not describe the whole proceeding as confidential.

name: Minnesota
agency: Minnesota Department of Public Safety, Office of Justice Programs, Crime Victims Reimbursement Board
statute_citation: Minn. Stat. 611A.51 to 611A.68; Minn. Stat. 609.35 (exam costs); Minn. R. ch. 3050
coverage_notes: Program pages on dps.mn.gov load their FAQ accordion text by script, so the saved page snapshot has only headings, phone, and history; rules lean on the statute, Minn. R. 3050.3200, the brochure, the application form, the mileage form, and the program's own October 2025 training slides. The exam statute caps state payment to the provider at $1,400 adjusted annually for inflation since January 1, 2024; that is a provider payment cap, not a survivor limit, so it is not recorded as an expense_cap. Not found: no dollar cap on medical (the board sets a payment percentage each fiscal year under Minn. R. 3050.3700 and 3050.3800); transportation is paid at the federal mileage rate with no dollar cap found; no coverage for security found (slides list security systems as not covered); the statute sets no emergency award amount; the counseling limit appears only in the training slides, not in a published fee schedule. How to file: the application form (MN-S10, Rev. 5/24, still the live version) lists the mailing address, fax, and email; the program page links the online Victim Services Portal. No in-person filing method and no processing time or decision deadline was found in the statute or program sources.
researcher_notes: Disagreement: Minn. Stat. 611A.52, subd. 8(b)(7) covers moving, storage, and phone and utility installation fees up to $1,000 per claim when a move is needed for safety, but the program's 2025 training slides (MN-S12, slide 33) list moving expenses as non-covered (the slides' non-covered list is recorded as MN-EXC-SECURITY, MN-EXC-CLOTHING, and MN-EXC-LEGAL; moving is deliberately not recorded as excluded). The statute wins per SCHEMA rule 3, so MN-CAP-RELOCATION is kept; the survivor should confirm with the board. The counseling $7,500 limit, crime scene cleanup $10,000 limit, misconduct waiver for sexual assault, and residency statement come only from the 2025 training slides, whose PDF text extraction is partly garbled; the quoted strings were checked as clean. Minn. R. 3050.3800 says the board resets counseling and medical limits each fiscal year. The slides also say evidentiary exams are not paid by the reimbursement program because the Sexual Assault Exam Payment Program pays them. The OVC directory still uses the old name, Crime Victims Reparations Board (renamed Reimbursement Board in 2023). Phones: 651-201-7300 and toll free 888-622-8799. Review pass: MN-REPORT-3 is a cooperation rule, not an alternative to the police report, so its alternatives list is empty. The counseling, cleanup, and alternative healing limits come from the slides and are treated as per claim; the slides do not say per claim or per victim. The slides also say counseling is paid at 70 percent, dental at 90 percent, and medical at 60 percent of the bill with the provider writing off the rest. The application form says the 30-day report has exceptions for child abuse and sexual assault. Packet step: MN-S10 is the current application PDF (same size as the live file, last modified March 2026); it has 53 fillable AcroForm fields. The mail, fax, and email rules quote the form's 'Complete and submit to' box. The online rule quotes the program page's link text; the URL itself is the href on that page, not printed in the snapshot text. The program page's accordion (in the raw HTML only) says the signed application may be mailed, faxed, or emailed. The Board itself obtains the police report and medical records using the signed releases, so those are not recorded as documents the survivor must include. Privacy step: Safe at Home (Minn. Stat. ch. 5B, Secretary of State) is the address confidentiality program; the SOS page (MN-S15) names sexual assault survivors, and Minn. Stat. 5B.02(e) (MN-S13) defines an eligible person to include a victim of sexual assault, with Minnesota residency or intent to reside within 60 days and excluding registered predatory offenders. The SOS page says enrollment goes through an Application Assistant; the statute (5B.03, MN-S14) says applications are filed with the secretary of state, certification lasts four years, and the secretary designates one mailing address for participants. Record confidentiality: Minn. Stat. 611A.57, subd. 6 makes claims investigative data under section 13.39 while open and private data on individuals after the claim closes, but the board may forward claim forms and reports to local law enforcement under 611A.67. Separately, Minn. Stat. 609.35(d) (MN-S5) makes sexual assault exam payment requests private data. The application form (MN-S10) also tells applicants their claim is confidential.

name: Missouri
agency: Missouri Department of Public Safety, Office for Victims of Crime
statute_citation: RSMo 595.010 to 595.075; forensic exams RSMo 595.220
coverage_notes: No minimum loss, emergency award, or police-report time limit appears in RSMo 595.010 to 595.075 or the DPS pages saved. The RSMo 595.010(12) definition of 'emergency service' (cash grants up to $100) belongs to victim services, not a CVC emergency award, so it is not recorded. No per-expense cap was found for counseling, medical, transportation, or security; relocation is listed as not payable. Transportation and security costs are not listed as covered or excluded. The program's Q and A PDF (cvc-qa.pdf) returned 404. No official source states a processing time for a decision or payment; the guidelines only give claimants 30 days to answer requests for information. RSMo 595.037 makes CVC claim information open to the public by default; sexual assault claims are closed and confidential only on a department determination, so record confidentiality for survivors is conditional, not automatic.
researcher_notes: Statute text is from revisor.mo.gov (595.010, 595.015, 595.020, 595.025, 595.030, 595.035 effective 28 Aug 2018; 595.220 effective 28 Aug 2020). Exam billing: RSMo 595.220.6 says eligible forensic exam charges are billed to and paid by DPS and the victim may not be charged; the statute does not mention insurance, while the DPS SAFE page and SAFE fact sheet say health insurance may be billed secondary, so insurance_billing is 'allowed' per the agency. The SAFE fact sheet adds that exams can be anonymous and that medical treatment (STI/HIV prophylaxis, emergency contraception, wound care, etc.) may be billed to the patient and then claimed from CVC. 11 CSR 30-12.010 sets provider reimbursement maximums for SAFE exams (saved as MO-S16) but these are not survivor-facing caps. The guidelines page states lost wages were capped at $200/week for crimes before Aug. 28, 2015 and $400/week after; only the current statutory $400 is recorded. The online application is reached from the CVC page; the PDF form (812-1321, rev. 10-18) is linked as 'CVC Application and Guide'. Toll-free 1-800-347-6881 also appears on the fact sheet and application. Cooperation with law enforcement is required unless good cause (RSMo 595.015.4); an arrest or conviction is not required (RSMo 595.025.3(1)). Reviewer: the brochure says out-of-state crimes must be filed in that state, but RSMo 595.020.5 lets a Missouri resident apply in Missouri when the place of the crime has no program that would cover them; the statute controls. The insurance_billing value 'allowed' rests on the DPS SAFE page and SAFE fact sheet only; RSMo 595.220.6 and 11 CSR 30-12.010 are silent on billing the survivor's insurance (the regulation bars insurance billing only for child physical abuse exams). The brochure and fact sheet also list clothing among costs CVC cannot pay. How to file: the saved application (MO-S6, form 812-1321 rev. 10-18, still the file DPS links as 'CVC Application and Guide', 192 fillable AcroForm fields) prints the old mailing address P.O. Box 749, Jefferson City, Missouri 65102-0749. Current DPS pages, the 1/2024 brochure, and the compensation checklist (MO-S17) all give P.O. Box 1589, Jefferson City, MO 65102-1589, so the mail rule uses the newer address. The CVC page says victims 'complete an online application', but its 'online application' link points back to the same CVC page and two searches found no separate portal; the online rule's target is that page, where the fillable PDF is posted. The brochure lists email (CVC@dps.mo.gov) and fax ((573) 526-4940) only for requesting an application or contacting the program, not for submitting one, so no email or fax submission rule is recorded. A police report is not something the applicant attaches: the form asks for the report number and agency, and the fact sheet says CVC requests documentation from law enforcement itself. Address confidentiality: RSMo 589.660 to 589.681 create the Secretary of State's Address Confidentiality Program (the Secretary's office brands it Safe at Home, but its page at sos.mo.gov/safeathome was blocked and could not be saved, so the statutory name is used). Eligibility expressly includes victims of rape and sexual assault who fear future harm; the application must be signed by a registered application assistant, and certification lasts four years with renewal. Record confidentiality: RSMo 595.037.1 says all information submitted on a CVC claim and any hearing 'shall be open to the public' except listed claims, which include rape, sodomy, or sexual abuse claims when the department determines confidentiality is in the victim's best interest, claims where the victim is a minor, and claims where disclosure would hurt apprehension or trial of an untried assailant; 595.037.2 lets the department close any record or hearing in the interest of justice. Tend should not tell Missouri survivors their claim is confidential by default.

name: Mississippi
agency: Office of the Mississippi Attorney General, Bureau of Victim Assistance, Crime Victim Compensation Division
statute_citation: Miss. Code Ann. 99-41-1 to 99-41-31 (Mississippi Crime Victims' Compensation Act); forensic exam: Miss. Code Ann. 99-37-25; rules: 3 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 1
coverage_notes: No minimum dollar loss appears in Miss. Code Ann. 99-41 sections read or in the administrative rules; the rules only say a claimant must show an economic loss. No source covers childcare or clothing/bedding replacement, and none expressly excludes them, so they are not found rather than excluded. Relocation and temporary housing are limited to domestic violence victims in imminent danger; the rules define domestic violence to include rape and sexual battery between current or former spouses or partners, dating partners, household or family members, so a survivor assaulted by a stranger or acquaintance would not qualify for those two benefits. The statute (99-41-23) and the 2025 program materials set no expense caps for relocation, housing, transportation, security or cleanup; those amounts come from the administrative rules.
researcher_notes: Statute text is from Justia's 2025 Mississippi Code because Mississippi does not host its own code; the 2025 brochure and Dec 2025 application match it. Conflict: the administrative rules (R. 104) still say a child sexual abuse claim must be filed by the child's twenty-first birthday, but the current text of Miss. Code Ann. 99-41-17(1)(b) (Justia 2025) says twenty-fifth, and the 2020 FAQ, 2025 brochure and Dec 2025 application all agree with the statute, so the statute is used. The administrative rules say they reflect legislation through the 2008 session, so they predate later statutory amendments; every rule-based cap used here (transportation $500, court travel $1,000, relocation $2,000, temporary housing $500, security repairs $1,000, cleanup $1,000) is repeated in the 2025 brochure and Dec 2025 application, except tuition ($2,000, also in the 2020 FAQ; the application lists tuition loss without an amount) and the advance award ($500, only in the rules). The forensic exam statute (99-37-25) says the survivor may still be billed for further medical services not needed for the investigation; those may be claimed through compensation if the claim is otherwise eligible (R. 301(9)). The exam payment rules say survivors covered by Medicaid, Medicare, Tricare, VA or CHIP are billed to that program first, and the provider may not pass any remaining balance to the survivor (R. 602(2), 604(6)). Exam payment caps per the rules: $350 medical personnel, $450 facility, $200 labs, within $1,000 per case. The exam payment does not require a police report, but a compensation claim does require a report within 72 hours or good cause. The 2020 FAQ (MS-S2) is older; its caps match the 2025 brochure except it lists tuition loss and execution travel, which the rules also cover. The phone 800-829-6766 is confirmed by the OVC state directory and the program pages; local number is 601-359-6766. Funeral cap ($6,500, 99-41-5(a)(iii)) added in review; funeral transportation ($800) is a separate limit in the same clause and is not encoded. How to file: the program page (MS-S1) links an online application on the AG portal (portal.ago.ms.gov, which blocked automated saving, so the target URL comes from the link on MS-S1); the Dec 2025 paper application (MS-S4) says to mail it to the letterhead address, P.O. Box 220 Jackson, MS 39205, and the 2025 brochure (MS-S3) says it can be mailed or faxed using the form's details (fax 601.576.4445). The brochure also says notarization is no longer necessary. The victimassistance@ago.ms.gov email is for questions, not for filing, so no email submission rule. The application PDF has no AcroForm fields (field_count 0), so it must be printed and filled by hand. No police report copy is required from the applicant: the form asks for the law enforcement agency and police incident report number, and the FAQ says the office requests the full offense report from law enforcement. Documents only for deceased victims (itemized funeral and burial expenses, tax return and proof of dependency) are not encoded. The 90-day decision time is from the 2020 FAQ (MS-S2); no newer source states a processing time. The Address Confidentiality Program (Miss. Code Ann. 99-47-1) is run by the Attorney General's office and is described in Chapter 07 of the same administrative rules (MS-S6): Rule 700 says it serves residents who are victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, and Rule 703 says applicants submit the application to the Office of the Attorney General, Victim Compensation Division, and that the assault need not have occurred in Mississippi. Registered sex offenders are not eligible. Compensation records are confidential under Miss. Code Ann. 99-41-31 (MS-S11), which also bars disclosing information about applicants without their written consent; the compensation application (MS-S4) cites the same section.

name: Montana
agency: Montana Department of Justice, Office of Victim Services
coverage_not_found: ["expense_cap for counseling for primary victims (current amount not verified)","expense_cap for lost_wages as a dollar amount","relocation","security","minimum_loss","insurance billing rule for the forensic exam"]
coverage_notes: Montana has no fixed dollar cap on lost wages for employed victims; MCA 53-9-128(1) pays 66 2/3% of wages up to one-half the state's average weekly wage, and 53-9-128(7)(a) caps victims who were employable but not employed at $100 per week. ARM 23.15.306(3) limits primary-victim counseling to 12 consecutive months or $2,000 with extensions available, but the same rule's secondary-victim limit ($2,000) has been superseded by the statute ($5,000), and the DOJ page names no primary-victim cap, so I did not encode a primary-victim counseling cap. I found no relocation, security, or minimum-loss provision. Neither the statute nor FREPP pages say whether the survivor's insurance may be billed for the exam.
researcher_notes: Total cap of $25,000 comes from the DOJ program page; the statute itself only caps death cases at $25,000 (MCA 53-9-128(5)). Reporting: adult survivors must report to law enforcement within 72 hours unless good cause is shown (ARM 23.15.103 lists factors such as the reasonableness of the delay and incapacity); there is no statutory alternative such as a forensic exam or advocate report. The exam itself does not require a report: unreported exams are paid by FREPP (MCA 46-15-411(2); DOJ FREPP page). ARM 23.15.402(1) (2005) says FREPP requires the exam within 72 hours and that the victim choose not to report. The current DOJ FREPP page does not repeat the 72-hour condition; the state rule is now shown as its own rule, and the DOJ page gives no time window. MCA 46-15-411(3) and the FREPP page say treatment of physical injuries from the assault is not covered by the exam payment and may be billed to the survivor; CVC may still cover such medical costs under MCA 53-9-128(2). ARM rules were saved from Cornell LII because the Secretary of State ARM site is script-driven. Reviewer note: MCA 53-9-103(3)(b) and (6)(a) define criminally injurious conduct and victim in terms of bodily injury or death, while the DOJ page describes a primary victim as someone who suffered direct physical or emotional harm; a survivor without a physical injury should confirm eligibility with the office. MT-CAP-2 uses the non-standard param applies_to: secondary_victims; the $5,000 counseling cap does not apply to the primary victim under the statute. How to file: the only submission method the official sources state is mail to P.O. Box 201410, Helena, MT 59620-1410 (Request a Claim Form page; the 12-25 claim form also carries a postage-paid business reply panel). The OVS contact block lists fax (406) 444-5335 and an email address, but no source says claims may be filed by fax or email, and the email is obfuscated in the saved snapshot, so I did not add fax or email submission rules. There is no online filing; the page's online request only mails a blank form. The claim form PDF (MT-S6, Version 10/2025) has no AcroForm fields, so it is printed and filled by hand. The 60-day processing time is a stated goal, not a guarantee. Address confidentiality: the DOJ Office of Victim Services runs the Address Confidentiality Program (substitute address plus free confidential first-class mail forwarding); the program page lists sexual assault among the qualifying victimizations and requires Montana residency. Record confidentiality: MCA 53-9-107(1) makes the compensation office's records open to public inspection by default; only personal, medical, or similar information whose release would be an unreasonable invasion of privacy is exempt under 53-9-107(3)(a), and the party seeking disclosure carries the burden. This is weaker than a blanket confidentiality statute, so the app should not tell survivors their claim file is fully sealed. The 12-25 claim form's release language also says the program will keep confidential information it receives confidential.

name: North Carolina
agency: North Carolina Department of Public Safety, Office of Victim Compensation Services (Crime Victims Compensation Commission)
statute_citation: N.C. Gen. Stat. 15B-1 to 15B-26; forensic exams: N.C. Gen. Stat. 143B-1200
coverage_notes: No minimum loss: the old minimum in G.S. 15B-11(e) was repealed in 1998 and nothing replaced it in the saved text. No emergency award found in Chapter 15B or 14B NCAC 09 Section .0300 (only partial payments under 14B NCAC 09 .0305). The statute gives no police-report alternative for sexual assault; it allows a report after six months only for good cause. Relocation and security are not listed as accepted or excluded. The $3,000 per-family counseling cap in G.S. 15B-2(1) applies only to immediate family members of child victims of rape, sexual assault, or domestic violence (and homicide families), so it is not recorded as a cap on the survivor's own counseling. Locks, doors, and windows appear only as part of crime scene cleanup on the agency page (NC-CLEAN-1), so no separate security rule is recorded.
researcher_notes: Statutes pulled from ncleg.gov (current through Session Laws 2026-53 per section history). Medical, counseling, and remedial care are paid at 66 2/3% of the provider's usual charge, which the provider must accept as payment in full (G.S. 15B-2(1)). Economic loss must be incurred within one year of the crime (two years for victims 18 or younger, with an exception for new medical or counseling costs), G.S. 15B-11(a)(2). The agency FAQ (NC-S5) says the two-year filing deadline has exceptions for the unreported sexual assault of a minor child and for missing persons later found to be homicide victims; I did not find that exception in the saved statute text. NC-DEAD-3 shows the FAQ's sentence in its own words, as the program's statement, and the engine keeps the statute's two years. The Rape Victim Assistance Program pays providers up to $1,500 per exam (physician or SANE $600, facility $500, other $400) under G.S. 143B-1200(d); that is a payment limit to providers, not a cost to the survivor, so it is not encoded as a survivor cap. Administrative rules (14B NCAC 09 .0301-.0305) set procedure only, no caps or rates. The agency 'Not Accepted' list includes 'Travel', recorded as excluded transportation. How to file: the agency page (NC-S5) gives an online portal and a mail address; the online start point is recorded as ncdps.gov/4victims because that is the address written in the saved text (the 'Start an Application' and log-in links in NC-S5.html point to https://victim-comp.ncdps.gov/users/sign_in, which does not appear as text). The paper application (NC-S8, the January 2026 version at program.application_pdf_url) ends with 'Please mail to' the same 4232 Mail Service Center address and lists a fax number, 919-715-4209, as contact information; it does not say applications may be faxed, so no fax submission rule is recorded. NC-S8 is a fillable AcroForm with 116 fields. The application also asks warrant-based cases to submit a copy of the warrant, which is covered by NC-DOC-2 (report or warrant). No photo ID or proof of residency is asked for; non-residents can apply for crimes in North Carolina. Address confidentiality: North Carolina's Address Confidentiality Program is in the Office of the Attorney General (G.S. Chapter 15C). G.S. 15C-2(2) names victims of 'sexual offense' as covered, and G.S. 15C-2 defines a victim of a sexual offense by reference to Article 7B of Chapter 14, so covers_sexual_assault is true. The program is for victims who have or will confidentially relocate in North Carolina (G.S. 15C-4(c)(4)), and the application must be made with an application assistant. Record confidentiality: G.S. 15B-8.1(b) makes personal information, claim disposition information (except the total award), medical information, and law enforcement records confidential; other Division records are open to public inspection, and the total amount awarded is not confidential.

name: North Dakota
agency: North Dakota Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, Division of Adult Services
statute_citation: N.D.C.C. ch. 54-23.4; N.D. Admin. Code art. 94-03; N.D.C.C. 12.1-34-07 (exam costs)
coverage_not_found: ["minimum_loss","expense_cap:relocation","expense_cap:security","covered_expense:relocation","covered_expense:security","covered_expense:temporary_housing","expense_cap:medical (no overall medical cap; only item sub-caps)","application_pdf_url","reporting_requirement:alternatives for sexual assault","address_confidentiality"]
coverage_notes: No general minimum loss was found; the only threshold is that a claimant must be unable to work at least three days to get work loss benefits (N.D. Admin. Code 94-03-03-13(2)(c)). No relocation, security, or temporary housing benefit appears in the statute, rules, or program pages. No sexual-assault-specific alternative to the 96-hour police report was found; late reports can be excused only for good cause. The application is online only (portalapps.nd.gov); no application PDF was found, so application_pdf_url is null. Medical has no overall cap but sub-caps: eyeglasses $500, alternative medical services $1,000, chiropractic or massage $1,200, cosmetic reconstructive procedures $5,000 (94-03-03-08(2)), and medical and dental services must be provided within two years of the crime. Counseling must fall within a two-year period beginning on the date of the first session (94-03-03-10(3)(b)). Home health services are capped at $300 per week and $4,800 total and must be provided within four months of the crime (94-03-03-11); a service animal is capped at $1,000 (94-03-03-12). The program page says the crime must be reported within 96 hours 'of the crime or discovery of the crime'; the statute and rule count 96 hours from the occurrence, so the engine follows the statute. address_confidentiality: North Dakota has no state address confidentiality program; the Minnesota Secretary of State Safe at Home 'Other States' directory (sos.mn.gov) lists 'North Dakota No Program', the Missouri Secretary of State and NOVA state ACP lists have no North Dakota entry, and no North Dakota statute or agency page for one was found. record_confidentiality: N.D.C.C. 54-23.4-17 makes division records on compensation applications and awards confidential (ND-REC-1); the program page (ND-S2) also says claim information is confidential and exempt from disclosure under that section.
researcher_notes: Statute text is the official ndlegis.gov Century Code PDF; admin rules are the official ndlegis.gov Article 94-03 PDFs (effective January 1, 2017). The program page agrees with the statute on the $25,000 total cap, the $300 per week wage cap, the 96-hour report, and the one-year filing deadline; the page states the wage cap as 'up to 16 weeks' and the rule as a $4,800 maximum (same total). Filing deadline runs from the date of the police report, not the crime. Work loss is limited to four months from the crime and is not paid while sick or annual leave is available. Travel requires at least 150 miles round trip and vehicle rental is capped at $30 per day. Contributory misconduct rule 94-03-03-05 lists conduct that requires denial; Tend shows conduct rules as information only. Reviewer: N.D.C.C. 12.1-34-07(2) separately bars charging a child forensic exam (criminal sexual conduct, physical abuse, or neglect) to the child or parent, and is recorded as ND-EXAM-CHILD. The program page says the application is online only (portalapps.nd.gov/docr/cvc-application/), so application_form is null with fillable false and field_count 0; the portal page could not be saved (blocked or empty, also through Chrome), so the application's own field list comes from the CVC Application Tips PDF (ND-S6). Box 1898, Bismarck, ND 58502-1898, fax 701-328-0309, and DOCRcompensation@nd.gov only as contact and correspondence details, and the employer and physician work-loss forms (ND-S10, ND-S11) are returned by mail, email, or fax. Supporting documents come from the 94-03-03 verification rules and the DOCR forms. Processing time (2 to 4 weeks) is from the program page. Added 81-1822(3) (no award if the victim's own criminal violation caused or contributed to the injury) as information only; the program says contributory conduct is never used to screen sexual assault claims (NE-S17). The wage rule NE-WAGE-1 is 'more than seven' consecutive days, so 7 days exactly does not qualify; it appears only on the Oct 2023 application form, not in the statute or regulation. 81-1823's $25,000 cap is 'Except as provided in section 81-1813', which was not saved. Submission is by mail or email per the program page and pamphlet; the fax number appears only in the application's return-to block next to the phone number, so NE-SUBMIT-3 is a reasonable reading rather than an explicit instruction. The program page lists the mailing address as Nebraska Crime Commission, 301 Centennial Mall South, P.O. Box 94946, Lincoln, NE 68509-4946; the application uses the shorter PO Box address, which I used. No online portal or in-person filing is stated. The 2023 FAQ (NE-S13) asks for 3 payroll stubs from just before the incident and an employer statement, while the Oct 2023 application asks for pay stubs for the missed periods and says CVR contacts the employer itself; I followed the application.
