No online filing portal was found. The office address on NV-S3 is where applicants can get help in person; no source says applications may be dropped off there, so in_person is not encoded. Documents: NV-S9 says to submit whatever documents you have now and send more later, and says eligible applicants will be sent a checklist of specific documents for each benefit; the lost wage section says a social security number must be included. Processing time comes from NRS 217.110(2) (60 days after receipt of the application, with a 5-day denial window when ineligibility is apparent); the 2020 State Plan 600.1 says the same 60 days. Confidential Address Program: NRS 217.462 to 217.471 (in NV-S5) set up the fictitious address program run by the Division of Child and Family Services (the Division is defined in NRS 217.400); administration moved there from the Attorney General in 2017, and the Attorney General's old CAP pages still show up in search, so the DCFS page (NV-S10) is used. NV-S10 says approved participants are enrolled for four years and lists the program's phone and email for finding a Certified Advocate; these are not encoded as params. NV-S10's eligibility list says applicants need specific evidence of victimization, and NRS 217.462(4) gives a conviction record or a protective order as examples, which may be a barrier for survivors who never reported. Record confidentiality: NRS 217.105 makes claim information confidential with three exceptions (applicant or attorney request, necessary administration of the chapter, court order); NRS 217.110 separately covers availability and confidentiality of law enforcement reports used in a claim and is not encoded.

name: New York
agency: New York State Office of Victim Services (OVS)
statute_citation: N.Y. Executive Law Article 22 (sections 620 to 635); 9 NYCRR Part 525; Public Health Law 2805-i
coverage_notes: total_cap: Article 22 sets no overall maximum award; it caps specific categories (lost earnings, relocation, property, etc.) and medical and counseling costs have no dollar cap in the statute. I did not record a total cap rather than infer one. Counseling rates: no per-session counseling fee cap was found in Executive Law 631 or in 9 NYCRR 525.3 or 525.12; 525.12(g)(4) lets OVS require proof that counseling is crime-related when a claim is filed more than one year after counseling began. minimum_loss: no minimum out-of-pocket loss requirement was found in the statute sections read. Security: covered for new or enhanced devices with a physician, counselor, or DA statement (525.12(g)(3)); no dollar cap found apart from the $2,500 crime scene securing cap. Financial difficulty: Exec. Law 631(6)(a) requires a finding of financial difficulty except for emergency awards and awards under ten thousand dollars (not a schema category). Reporting: the old one-week police reporting rule is no longer in Exec. Law 631(1); the current text accepts records of a support agency for survivors of crime. OVS pages say the Crime Verification Form is accepted only for claims filed on or after December 31, 2025. Reviewer additions: 9 NYCRR 525.12(h)(9) (LII text, last amended 2022) says direct-reimbursement exam expenses must relate to services within 120 hours of the incident, waived for a child victim or for good cause, and no kit reimbursement past 120 hours; the current Exec. Law 631(13) and the March 2026 OVS provider billing manual do not state this window, so it is not encoded as a rule. The per-item clothing, bedding, communication and transportation-item limits in 525.12(n)(1)-(4) do not apply when OVS finds the property is related to the victim's health or safety (525.12(n)(6)); the $2,500 statutory property cap still applies. The protective-order, victim services provider, and medical or mental health provider alternatives in Exec. Law 631(1)(c)(iii) are conditioned in the statute on the victim being unable to report to or cooperate with police for health or safety reasons; the OVS update page (NY-S7) describes the Crime Verification Form without that condition. processing_time: no saved OVS page, application, or statute section states a time for a decision or payment, so none is recorded.
researcher_notes: Statute text is from the NY Senate Open Legislation site (fetched via Chrome). 9 NYCRR text is from Cornell LII because the official Westlaw NYCRR site is script-heavy; LII shows the 525.12 amendment history through Oct 12, 2022, and its funeral cap ($6,000) is older than the current statute ($12,000 in Exec. Law 631(2)), so for any conflict the statute wins. Effective dates from OVS update pages: three-year filing deadline and Crime Verification Form alternative to police reports apply starting December 31, 2025; filing deadline previously shorter. Exec. Law 631(13)(b) also sets provider reimbursement ceilings for the exam ($800 / $1,200 / $2,500); these are provider rates, not survivor-facing, so I did not encode them. The OVS FRE page says claims received on or after February 3, 2026 are paid by a new OVS fee schedule. PHL 2805-i(1) has two versions of the no-billing paragraph (lettered (d) until May 9, 2027 and (g) after); the quoted text is identical in both. Expense caps with per='item' (clothing, communication items) are per-item limits from 9 NYCRR 525.12(n); per='item' is outside the schema's listed values but is what the regulation says. A phone would most plausibly fall under 'ability to communicate', but the regulation does not name phones. Essential personal property awards for adults generally require a physical injury; sex offense victims are presumed physically injured under Exec. Law 626(1). The older OVS FAQ page and 2022 guideline PDFs state superseded rules (one-week reporting, one-year filing, $500 property cap), so I did not use them. How to file: the English application link on the OVS page (ovs.ny.gov/compensation_application_english) still redirects to the Feb. 2026 fillable PDF saved as NY-S4 (552 AcroForm fields), so that is the newest version. Submission targets come from the application's contact section: mail to the Albany AE Smith Building address and email to OVSIntake@ovs.ny.gov; online filing is through OVS Compass (program.apply_url). The OVS page (NY-S1) also lists a Brooklyn office at 55 Hanson Place for the Compensation Division, but the application says to mail documents to the Albany address, so only Albany is encoded. No fax or in-person filing method is stated. The application also says documents can be sent later if not ready, and the OVS page says OVS may later ask for birth or death certificates, marriage licenses, insurance Explanations of Benefits, and receipts depending on the claim; those on-request items are not encoded as required documents. Photo ID, proof of residency, and wage verification are not requested up front; for lost wages the application says OVS contacts the employer. Address confidentiality: Exec. Law 108 (NY-S21) makes victims of a sexual offense (Penal Law article 130 and 255.25 to 255.27, including threats or attempts) eligible for the Department of State Address Confidentiality Program; applicants affirm they left their residence because of the acts and fear for their safety (108(2)(a)(i)), applications are filed with the office of the secretary (108(2)(c)), designated state, local or nonprofit agencies assist applicants (108(3)), and certification lasts four years (108(2)(e)). The DOS ACP pages (NY-S22, NY-S23) still describe eligibility as victims of domestic violence only and say participation is limited to New York State residents; the statute is broader and wins, so covers_sexual_assault is true from the statute. The enroll text and contact details come from the DOS apply page (NY-S23). Record confidentiality: Exec. Law 633(1) (NY-S20) exceptions are legitimate criminal justice requests (where the victim reported to a victim services provider instead of police, OVS may not share identifying information), judicial subpoenas, requests by the victim or claimant or their authorized representative, and purposes necessary for administering Article 22; 633(2) makes other OVS records (such as those under 631-a and 632-a) public; 633(3) keeps records that are confidential under other laws confidential.

name: Ohio
program_name: Ohio Victims of Crime Compensation Program
agency: Ohio Attorney General, Crime Victim Services Section
coverage_not_found: ["relocation","temporary_housing","transportation","security (standalone)","expense_cap for lost_wages","expense_cap for medical","expense_cap for counseling for the victim","reporting alternatives for sexual assault"]
coverage_notes: No statute, rule, or official page I could save sets a weekly wage cap, a per-session counseling cap for the victim, or any relocation, housing, or transportation benefit. The application lists 'Mileage' as a checkbox but I found no rule text describing it. Security repairs are covered only as part of crime scene cleanup (ORC 2743.51(T)(2), $750 per claim). The statute requires that the crime was reported to law enforcement at some point and lists no alternative (forensic exam, advocate, protective order) for sexual assault. The Attorney General's HTML program pages (Apply for Victims Compensation, SAFE Program) could not be saved by the fetch tool, so the application PDF and brochure stand in for them. Privacy (added Oct 3): Safe at Home is Ohio's address confidentiality program (ORC 111.41 to 111.47, Secretary of State). For compensation records I found only ORC 2743.62(A)(2)(a), which keeps already-confidential records (for example medical records) confidential in the AG's or Court of Claims' hands; I found no statute or official statement making the whole claim, application, or applicant identity confidential or exempt from public records law.
researcher_notes: Statutes are from codes.ohio.gov (ORC 2743.51, 2743.56, 2743.60 effective March 2, 2022 after S.B. 36). Disagreements: the AG brochure 'Crime Can Be Costly' (OH-S15, undated) says family counseling is capped at $2,500 per person or $7,500 per family, but ORC 2743.60(H) caps an (L)(2) immediate-family claimant at $5,000; I used the statute. The Court of Claims FAQ (OH-S12) still says certain serious criminal history disqualifies, but the AG's own Apply for Victims Compensation page (read during research but not savable with the fetch tool) says that as of March 2, 2022 criminal backgrounds are no longer disqualifiers, matching the amended ORC 2743.60. Exam billing: per the AG SAFE instructions (OH-S14), emergency contraception, pain medication, and treatment of injuries beyond the forensic exam may be billed to the patient or insurer; those costs can then be claimed as medical expenses. Ohio health care providers must report a sexual assault to police under ORC 2921.22 (an adult may stay unnamed), per OH-S14; I did not find authority saying that provider report satisfies the compensation reporting rule, so Tend should not assume it does. ORC 2743.521(B) (OH-S11) bars a medical provider that accepts payment through an award from billing the victim for those expenses. The application PDF lists phone 614-466-5610 and toll-free 877-584-2846 (877-5VICTIM); the OVC directory lists 614-466-5610. Reviewer: added OH-EXAM-5 to 7 and OH-CAP-6 from sources already saved. The free exam is limited to evidence collection: for adults the SAFE table makes procedures billable to the patient when the last incident was more than 96 hours earlier (absent documented extenuating circumstances), and with other injuries the ED level charge, physician charges, labs, scans, and HIV prophylaxis are listed as billable to the patient. OAC 109:7-1-02(C) lets the Attorney General raise the $632 and $2,500 amounts for inflation; the SAFE instructions still state $632, so I kept it, but the current figure could be higher. ORC 2743.60(F) and (I) also bar awards for crimes against adults while serving a prison sentence and suspend payment while a victim is incarcerated; there is no schema category for these. How to file (added Oct 3): the AG Apply for Victims Compensation page (OH-S16) lists online filing, mail, fax, and email. The fetch tool rejected that page as blocked because the site is ASP.NET and wraps all content in one <form>, which the tool strips; I saved the same Chrome snapshot with the tool's text extraction minus the form removal, so OH-S16.txt is that page's text. The online target is the 'Register and file' link in the saved HTML. ORC 2743.56(A) (OH-S4) says a mailed application counts as filed on its postmark date. The application PDF (OH-S9, same URL the Apply page links, modified June 2026) has 207 AcroForm fields. It asks for copies of 6 paychecks for lost wages, front and back of insurance cards, a death certificate for funeral claims, and a signed release; it does not tell applicants to attach bills, receipts, or a police report, so I did not add those. ORC 2743.59(E) (OH-S17) sets the 120-day decision limit, which the AG can extend in writing; no AG page states a typical processing time. A separate supplemental application exists for later expenses and was not saved. Privacy (added Oct 3): ORC 111.42(A)(3) (OH-S18) makes victims of rape or sexual battery eligible for Safe at Home; the Secretary of State page (OH-S20) also lists sexual assault and says participants must apply through a certified Application Assistant and get a substitute address for voter registration, government correspondence, and other official records. Certification lasts four years (ORC 111.42(E)); registered sex offenders are ineligible. Record confidentiality is narrow: ORC 2743.62(A)(2)(a) (OH-S19) only preserves the confidential status a record already had, and 2743.62(A)(2)(b) lets judges, magistrates, the claimant, and the AG refer to those records in hearings and written decisions. The Court of Claims page (OH-S12) says it keeps an electronic archive of Victims decisions back to 1977, so Tend should not tell Ohio users their claim is fully private. I did not find any ORC 149.43(A)(1) exemption naming compensation claim files.

name: Oklahoma
agency: Oklahoma District Attorneys Council, Victim Services Division, Crime Victims Compensation Board
coverage_notes: No dollar minimum loss was found; program pages only say there must be economic loss. Relocation, security, and temporary housing are not listed as allowable expenses in 21 O.S. 142.3 or on the program pages, and no cap for the victim's own lost wages was found beyond the overall cap. Medical services are limited to 80% of cost rather than a dollar cap. No statute was found that expressly bars a provider from billing the survivor for exam charges above the $800 fund limit. Address confidentiality comes from the Attorney General's ACP page (statutory basis 22 O.S. 60.14, not saved here); record confidentiality comes from 21 O.S. 142.9(G).
researcher_notes: Statutes (OSCN, 21 O.S. as amended by SB 420, eff. Nov 1, 2023) win over program pages. Conflicts: the DAC page and the 2019 claim form say the total cap is $20,000 ($40,000 with the wage add-on) and the filing deadline is one year; current 142.13(B) says $25,000 ($50,000) and 142.10(A)(1) says thirty months. The OCVC eligibility page says caregiver work loss is $2,000 but 142.13(A) and (K) say $3,000. 142.10(A)(1) still has a leftover phrase about extending 'beyond one (1) year' next to the new 30-month period. The Board may grant up to $25,000 beyond the base cap for wages or loss of support, with a hard ceiling of $50,000 under 142.13(B). The application PDF is the 2019 form and predates the 2023 changes; the online claim at ocvcapp.okvictimscomp.com is the primary route. OAC 185:10-1-4 still says one year and was not used. The filing_deadline rule uses a 'months' param because the schema only lists years or days. Exam: OAC 185:15-1-6(d) treats Medicaid or other federal programs as a collateral source that must deny first; private insurance is optional for the survivor and any insurance payment goes back to the fund (185:15-1-6(c)). Providers must stop debt collection once notified of a pending claim (21 O.S. 142.9(H)). Reviewer: the OCVC home page still says a claim should be filed within one year, and the eligibility page says 'within one (30) months'; the statute's 30 months controls. 142.3 on OSCN lists amendments only through 2007 even though its text mentions vehicle impound fees, so its history note may be incomplete. Vehicle impound fees are capped at $750 (142.13(L)) and homicide family crisis counseling at $3,000 (142.13(G)); neither was added as a rule because neither applies to a living sexual assault survivor. The DAC exam page says the $800 limit applies to assaults on or after November 1, 2023, so older assaults may fall under an earlier, lower limit that was not researched. How to file: the online portal (ocvcapp.okvictimscomp.com) is the main route; its page says written applications go by mail or fax, while the 2019 claim form says to print, sign, and then fax, email, or mail it, so email comes only from the form. The current printable application is still the June 2019 claim form (OK-S12), which the portal links; it is a flat PDF with no fillable fields (pypdf found 0), and the DAC page still links older 2016/2017 forms that were not used. No in-person filing method is stated. The police report is requested by the DA's Victim-Witness Coordinator, not attached by the survivor. Processing times come from program pages, not statute: the FAQ says 4 to 12 months overall, the DAC page says claims are docketed within 30 days of full documentation and paid within three weeks of approval. Privacy: the Oklahoma Attorney General runs the Address Confidentiality Program (OK-S26); its page lists sexual assault among covered crimes and says applicants must have recently relocated or be planning to move, and apply in person through a designated victim assistance program with an application assistant (no direct applications). Certification lasts four years per the page. The program's statutory basis is 22 O.S. 60.14, which was not saved. Claim records are confidential under 21 O.S. 142.9(G) (OK-S6), with discovery exceptions only for an APA appeal of a Board decision or a strict showing to a court. OAC 185:15-1-6(b) (OK-S20) also lets exam-fund survivors skip employment and insurance information to keep anonymity.

name: Oregon
agency: Oregon Department of Justice, Crime Victim and Survivor Services Division
statute_citation: ORS 147.005 to 147.367 (compensation); ORS 147.395 to 147.399 (SAVE Fund); OAR 137-076 and 137-084
coverage_notes: No minimum out-of-pocket loss appears in ORS 147.005 to 147.367 or OAR 137-076, so minimum_loss is left out rather than assumed to be zero. No security (locks, alarms) or temporary housing benefit was found. Relocation is listed as excluded on the program page, so there is no relocation cap. Oregon has no statute that makes compensation records confidential by default: ORS 147.115(1) makes applicant information public unless the department decides to keep it confidential, so record_confidentiality is recorded as conditional.
researcher_notes: Statute and rule text come from oregonlegislature.gov (ORS ch. 147, current edition with 2025 notes) and the Secretary of State OARD site (OAR 137-076 and 137-084, saved through the browser). Conflicts: (1) ORS 147.055 allows an emergency award up to $1,000, but the program page says CVC is unable to provide immediate financial assistance; the rule is kept because the statute governs, but in practice the program may not offer one. (2) OAR 137-084-0010(4) requires a complete SAFE Kit assessment within 84 hours of the assault for SAVE Fund payment, while the DOJ provider page lists 120 hours; the victim SAVE page says within seven days (matches the 168-hour partial assessment). (3) Statute sets transportation coverage when care is more than 30 miles away; agency pages say 60 miles roundtrip (consistent). OAR 137-076-0019(1)(e) states the rate as '.50 cents per mile'; the brochure says 50 cents per mile. (4) The FAQ says loss of support rose to $800/week; that applies to dependents of deceased victims only. Claims expire three years after the determination order (or at age 21 for minors), ORS 147.035(8). Toll-free number 1-800-503-7983 appears in the brochure. Under the SAVE FAQ, a survivor may choose to bill insurance instead of the SAVE Fund, in which case leftover copays go to a CVC application rather than the Fund. The limited counseling award ($5,000) is the path for survivors who never report and never get an exam or order. Strangulation (SKIT) exams are paid under ORS 147.035(2)(e) with a $5,000 maximum and are billed to insurance first, so they are not modeled as exam_no_bill. Reviewer: the SAVE Fund's $475 maximum (OAR 137-084-0020(1)(a)) is what the Fund pays the provider for an exam plus SAFE Kit collection, not a limit on what the survivor gets, and the provider cannot bill the survivor or insurance for the rest; it is therefore not modeled as an expense_cap. The limited counseling award (OR-CAP-COUNS-LTD, $5,000) and the parent lost wages cap (OR-CAP-WAGE-PARENT, $5,000) are conditional caps for applicants who do not meet eligibility and for parents of minor victims, not general caps on the victim's counseling or lost wages. How to file (added Oct 3): submission methods, documents, and timing come mainly from the 2026 fillable English application (OR-S7, 140 AcroForm fields), which is the newest version linked from the apply page. The apply page FAQ (OR-S5) gives the mailing address as '1162 Court St SE', but the 2026 application, the brochure, and the program page all say 1162 Court Street NE, so the mail rule uses NE. Page 2 of the application still lists the old email domain cvssd@doj.state.or.us; the instructions page uses cvssd@doj.oregon.gov, which is used here. The program page and brochure list fax 503-378-5738 as contact information but no source says to fax the application, so no fax submission rule was added. Decision timing differs by source: the 2026 application says 60 to 90 days, the FAQ says applicants are usually notified within 70 days, and the 2024 brochure says 45 to 60 days; the newest (application) is used. The application does not ask the survivor to attach a police report or medical records: it asks for the report number and provider details, and CVC requests medical records and police reports itself. Bills are submitted after the claim is accepted. Privacy (added Oct 3): Oregon's Address Confidentiality Program is run by the Oregon DOJ (not the Secretary of State) under ORS 192.820 to 192.868; ORS 192.822(1)(a) and 192.826(3) name victims of a sexual offense as eligible, and the DOJ page names survivors of sexual assault. Enrollment is only through a certified Application Assistant (a victim advocate designated by the Attorney General); the ACP FAQ says applicants must live in Oregon, be 18 or older (parents or guardians may apply for minors), and currently live at an address unknown to the perpetrator, so a recent confidential relocation is required, and participation lasts four years. ACP contact: P.O. Box 1108, Salem, OR 97308; 503-373-1323; toll-free in Oregon 1-888-559-9090; ACP@doj.oregon.gov. Record confidentiality is weak in Oregon: ORS 147.115(1) says applicant information is open to the public unless the department determines it should be confidential, with sexual offenses (rape, sodomy, sexual abuse) as one listed ground, and ORS 147.115(3) says board hearing records are public records. The 2026 application itself warns that 'this application may be subject to disclosure under public record law' (OR-S7, page 2), so Tend should tell Oregon survivors to ask CVC to keep their claim confidential under the sexual offense ground and avoid putting extra detail in the free-text field. Separately, ORS 147.397(5)(a) requires SAVE Fund exam providers to keep confidential the identity of victims who have not reported to police.

name: Pennsylvania
agency: Pennsylvania Commission on Crime and Delinquency (PCCD), Office of Victims' Services
statute_citation: Crime Victims Act, 18 P.S. 11.101 et seq. (compensation: 18 P.S. 11.701 to 11.710); 37 Pa. Code Chapter 411
coverage_not_found: ["expense_cap:security","covered_expense:security","excluded_expense:phones (no explicit statement; only general property exclusion)"]
coverage_notes: No source found that covers home security costs (locks, alarms, cameras); treat security as not covered unless the program confirms. Phones are not named anywhere; the general property loss/damage exclusion applies. The statute's emergency award limit is 'a rate set by the Office of Victims' Services'; the $5,000 figure comes from 37 Pa. Code 411.17 and matches the 2025 manual. Relocation lodging is $75 per day (PA-RELOC-4); relocation vehicle rental is $30 per day (37 Pa. Code 411.42(f)), not encoded separately. Travel caps (car rental $30/day, meals $28/day for trips of 50+ miles) are taken from the 2025 manual because the matching list in 37 Pa. Code 411.42(g) is introduced by a clause about death and funeral travel and reads ambiguously. Filing: the claim form (July 2024, the version linked from the PA.gov apply page) lists the mailing address, email, and the DAVE online portal; the PA.gov page also lists the Crime Victims App for online filing. The form's fax number (717-787-4306) is listed only as contact info and the manual mentions fax only for advocates sending supplemental bills, so no fax submission rule was added. No in-person filing method is stated.
researcher_notes: Act 77 of 2022 changes (5-year filing deadline, 'promptly' reporting instead of 72 hours, $50 minimum loss, 701.1 counseling claims, conduct not considered for counseling) apply to crimes on or after 9/8/2022; for older crimes the program says to contact it (2-year deadline and 72-hour reporting applied before). 37 Pa. Code Chapter 411 was last amended in 2009 and still references some pre-2022 limits (for example a 1-year FRE provider deadline that is consistent with the 2024 FRE protocol); where regulations and statute differ the statute controls. The PA.gov page says 'The crime must have occurred in Pennsylvania', while the statute's definitions (18 P.S. 11.103) also cover Pennsylvania residents harmed outside the state when the other location's program is ineligible under VOCA; the manual narrows this to foreign countries without a program and international terrorism. Insurance: providers must bill the survivor's insurance first for the exam unless the survivor (or person responsible) asks that insurance not be billed (18 P.S. 11.707(h)(1); FRE protocol B.2), so insurance_billing is recorded as 'allowed' with a survivor opt-out. The PA.gov transportation flyer says 'A maximum payment of $35,000 per direct victim can be reimbursed for transportation expenses'; that is just the overall cap and is not encoded. The English VCAP brochure PDF is image-only and was not saved. Counseling for a minor whose insurance is held by the alleged perpetrator or a non-supportive caretaker may be paid without billing that insurance (18 P.S. 11.707(b)(4.1)(i)). Reviewer: the PA.gov page says the claim must be filed 'within 5 years of the crime'; the statute (18 P.S. 11.702(b)(1)) runs it from discovery, which the rule follows. The 37 Pa. Code 411.42(d) health-item limit says 'each' device and 'will not exceed $1,000'; encoded per claim, but it may be read per item. FRE FAQ: if the survivor declines evidence collection the hospital may bill the survivor's insurance (Q14), and medications without an exam are not paid on the FRE claim (Q11); both can go on a standard claim. Application form: PA-S6 (VCAP long claim form, July 2024) is a flat PDF with no AcroForm fields (0 fields), so it is not fillable; a short claim form and a separate FRE claim form also exist but were not saved. The 2025 manual cover gives the PO Box ZIP as 17110-1167, while the claim form and the manual's own sample letters use 17108-1167; the submission rule follows the claim form. The applicant does not need to attach a police report: the claim process flyer says VCAP obtains the police report itself and sends verification forms to providers and employers; the form asks for the police department and incident number. The 12-week figure is from the PA.gov FAQ ('Most organizations process claims in 12 weeks or less'), not the statute. Payments to providers are released 2 to 4 weeks after approval (PA-S13). Address confidentiality: the OVA ACP page (PA-S14) lists sexual assault victims as eligible and says enrollment is online, through a local victim service program, or by calling OVA; the statute (23 Pa.C.S. 6703(a)) says eligible persons 'shall receive a confidential substitute address provided by the Office of Victim Advocate'. The statute's definition of 'victim of sexual assault' (23 Pa.C.S. 6702) lists specific offenses (18 Pa.C.S. 3121 rape, 3133, 4302, 6312, 6318, 6320) and 6704(2) requires an affidavit that the applicant fears future violent acts by the perpetrator, so eligibility under the statute is narrower than the agency page wording; OVA decides. ACP records, including applications and actual addresses, are confidential and exempt from the Right-to-Know Law (23 Pa.C.S. 6703(d)). Participants renew every 3 years per the OVA page. Record confidentiality: 18 P.S. 11.709(b) bars disclosure without the written consent of the direct victim or intervenor, except as otherwise provided by law; 11.709(c) still allows use in OVS appeal hearings, in enforcing section 1303, and in talking with the prosecutor about restitution. The Act 77 flyer (PA-S7) restates this.

name: Rhode Island
agency: Rhode Island Office of the General Treasurer
coverage_notes: No Rhode Island statute or official policy was found that bars billing the survivor or the survivor's insurance for a sexual assault forensic exam; the only official statement found is the Attorney General's bill of rights saying the exam cost is compensable through the CVCP regardless of reporting. No minimum loss was found. The relocation cap is in flux: the compiled statute (12-25-21.1(e)) and the current rule say $5,000, but a 2026 bill (H 8155) raised it to $8,000 and the amended rule effective 10/13/2026 (RI-S14) says $8,000, so no relocation dollar cap is recorded. Counseling hourly rates, the $1,000 travel cap, the 62% lost-earnings rule, the property exclusion, and the reporting rules appear in both the current rule (RI-S11) and the amended rule effective 10/13/2026 (RI-S14). No processing time for a decision or payment is stated in the program page, the application, or the rule; the only stated times are 30 days for a decision on reconsideration, which is not recorded. The address confidentiality program and record confidentiality rule were both found.
researcher_notes: Statute text is from the RI legislature's compiled General Laws site, which may not yet show 2026 session laws. The rule amendment effective 10/13/2026 says it implements 2026 changes to 12-25-20 and 12-25-21.1: hit-and-run serious bodily injury added, stalking victims allowed relocation or home-modification awards, larceny and the crime against nature offenses removed from the covered list, and emergency relocation raised to $8,000. The introduced H 8155 text only changes the relocation amount; it leaves the $1,000 home-safety cap and $25,000 total cap unchanged, but the enacted version was not saved, so RI-SECURITY-1 should be rechecked once the compiled statute updates. The AG page says exam compensation is available regardless of cooperation, while 12-25-19(d)(1)(i) lets the office weigh cooperation for other awards; statute wins for non-exam expenses. The program FAQ (RI-S8) also lists a DCYF report for minors and a no contact order for domestic violence victims as alternatives to a police report. Other caps in the rule not recorded as rules: eyeglasses $200, crime scene cleanup $2,000, burial $10,000, secondary victim counseling $1,500, group therapy at 40% of the individual rate, temporary housing $150 per night for up to 10 nights within relocation. Reviewer: the AG page says exam compensation is available regardless of reporting, but 12-25-22(a) only lets the office accept an exam in place of a police report when the exam was within 15 days of the crime, and the same AG page warns that not participating in the criminal justice system will likely limit compensation eligibility. A 2022 bill (S 2374) would have barred charging the survivor for the evidentiary exam (proposed 12-28.1-6), but chapter 12-28.1 does not exist in the compiled General Laws and 23-98-5 has no billing rule, so exam_no_bill stays not_found. researcher_notes: Statute text is the 2025 Tennessee Code via Justia (legislature/Lexis site not used). Total cap disagreement: T.C.A. 29-13-106(e) states $30,000 'except as provided in subsection (h)', and (h) indexes the cap to 105 percent of the national average, published by the State Treasurer on the Treasury website (not a rule, effective July 1). R. & Regs. 0300-02-.07 (rev. May 2025, TN-S14) says $34,200 for crimes on or after July 1, 2025 and contains a typo ('thirty-two thousand dollars ($32,900.00)'). The program page FAQ also still says $32,900. The lower, later Treasury-published $34,100 is recorded; confirm with the program. Medical and medical-related bills are paid at 75 percent of billed charges (T.C.A. 29-13-107(7)); a provider paid 75 percent must accept it as payment in full. Forensic exam reimbursement to the provider is capped at $1,000 and is full payment (29-13-118(d)); the provider files within 1 year of the exam. The SAFE provider page says medical treatment for injury may be billed to the patient, who may then claim compensation. Cooperation with police and prosecutors is required (29-13-109(f)) with an exception when cooperation is affected by age, psychological state, fear of retaliation, or other safety concerns (29-13-103(a)(4)). An arrest or conviction is not required (29-13-109(f)). Statute 29-13-108(b) says claims are filed in person or by mail; the Treasury says to apply through its online portal (linked as 'File a Claim' on the program page). Phone 833-867-3891 is the program's; the OVC directory lists 615-741-2734 for the Division of Claims and Risk Management. Reviewer (Oct 3, 2026): T.C.A. 29-13-106(h)(4)-(5) makes the Treasurer's website publication the operative cap and says it is not a rule, which supports $34,100 over the $34,200 in Rule 0300-02-.07. The live program page checked in Chrome on Oct 3, 2026 lists $34,100 for crimes on or after July 1, 2025 and shows no separate figure for July 1, 2026, even though (h)(2) calls for an annual comparison starting January 1, 2026; if a 2026 adjustment is published later, CAP-1 needs a new source. The same page says counseling 'may be considered for the victim up to the maximum award' (not saved; fetch_source.py --chrome returned 'blocked or empty'). T.C.A. 29-13-105(c) bars an award to a victim who was a member of the offender's family only if a benefit would go to the offender, and says it does not automatically disqualify such a victim. How to file (Oct 3, 2026): the Treasury takes claims online only (resource guide TN-S1 and program page TN-S15, whose File a Claim link goes to an Origami Risk incident-entry portal); there is no paper or PDF application, so program.application_form is {source_id: null, fillable: false, field_count: 0}. T.C.A. 29-13-108(b) still says claims are filed 'in person or by mail', but no saved source gives a mailing or walk-in address for claims, so no mail or in_person submission rule was added. The only address published is on the Employer's Statement (TN-S16, RDA-1178, a fillable PDF with 60 AcroForm fields): 502 Deaderick Street, Nashville, TN 37243-0202, where the employer sends that form. The online form must be finished in one session; supporting documents are uploaded as PDF or Word files. Criminal.Injury@tn.gov is published for advocates, not as a claim submission address. TN-S15 was saved by hand because fetch_source.py strips form elements and this DNN page sits inside one; raw bytes are the server's HTML and the sha256 matches. Address confidentiality: Tennessee's program is Safe at Home, run by the Secretary of State under T.C.A. 40-38-601 to 40-38-614 (statute calls it the address confidentiality program). 40-38-602(a) opens it to victims of rape, sexual battery, or another sexual offense at no cost; 40-38-602(b) gives a substitute address and bars disclosure of the participant's file; 40-38-602(f) and (j) make the participant's file and application not public records. The substitute address may not be used for property tax or recorded real property documents (40-38-602(d)). Registered sex, animal abuse, vulnerable-adult abuse, and drug offenders are ineligible (40-38-603). Under 40-38-604(a)-(b) the application is filed with an application assistant and needs either documentary evidence of a criminal case, an order of protection in effect, or a notarized statement from a licensed professional (attorney, social worker, therapist) that the applicant is in danger, plus a sworn statement, notarized signatures, and an address not in any public record or a move within 30 days before or 90 days after applying. A survivor who has not reported can still qualify through the professional's statement. Record confidentiality: T.C.A. 10-7-504(k) closes only four items about compensation applicants to the public (residential address, home and personal cell numbers, SSN, and the offense being compensated); the victim's name and other claim contents are not listed there, and no confidentiality section was found in T.C.A. 29-13-101 to 29-13-119. The Comptroller's 2018 list of Public Records Act exceptions (TN-S22) lists 10-7-504(k) as the Criminal Injuries Compensation Act exception.

The application instructions (WY-S6) say relocation applies only when the crime scene was the victim's home (domestic violence, homicide, sexual assault), so for a sexual assault at home the $500 limit is the likely one. The reported-exam no-bill policy sits under a heading for reports made without a compensation claim; DVS pays only SANE exam and evidence collection costs there. How to file: the posted Primary Victim Application (WY-S5, rev. 4/23, labeled SAMPLE) is a flat PDF with no form fields, so it is printed and filled by hand. The only submission method the sources state is mail to DVS in Cheyenne (the 'Return to' line on the authorization page). The fax number and email on the letterhead are contact details, not stated filing methods, so they are not encoded. The compensation page (WY-S1) says local victim service providers give out the application, help fill it in, and submit it to DVS; that route is the program's recommended path but has no matching submission method. No processing time is stated; the instructions (WY-S6) only say to call or email if there has been no letter or call within 30 days after mailing, which is a status-check prompt, not a decision time. Required documents also vary by expense type in the guidelines (gas and lodging receipts for travel, itemized lists for items taken as evidence, physician verification for lost wages past 30 days); only the general ones and the wage and counseling forms are encoded. Privacy: W.S. 1-40-107(d) (from the DVS-posted copy of the Act, WY-S4) makes claim file information that is subject to a confidentiality privilege confidential and not open to public inspection; the protection is tied to information already privileged under Wyoming law, so it is not a blanket rule covering every field on the application. Wyoming has no address confidentiality program, so no substitute-address rule is encoded. The closest thing found is W.S. 35-21-112, a court confidentiality order for a domestic violence victim's address in protection order proceedings, which is not a substitute-address program and was not saved or encoded. Separately, W.S. 6-2-309(m) (WY-S8) keeps sexual assault exam results confidential healthcare information unless the victim signs a release, which is about exam records, not compensation records.
